items.title: How to Argue in the Trump Era Without Losing Your Mind
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with his reaction to the shooting at the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Ontario on Yom Kippur. David discusses the rise of violence against Jews around the world, and why condemnations of anti-Semitic violence ring hollow when they come from people who spread myths about Jewish conspiracies. Then, David is joined by Jessica Tarlov, the co-host of The Five on Fox News and the Raging Moderates podcast. They talk about her new book, I Disagree: Winning Arguments Without Losing Friends , and how her upbringing helped shape her ability to disagree cordially. David and Jessica also discuss when to debate someone versus when to ignore them so as not to give them a platform. Finally, David ends the show with a review of the novel Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke. The following is a transcript of the episode: David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show. I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic. My guest this week will be Jessica Tarlov, co-host of the Fox News program The Five and author of the new book I Disagree: Winning Arguments Without Losing Friends. She’s also the co-host with Scott Galloway of the Raging Moderates podcast. The book for discussion this week will be a much-acclaimed new novel, Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke, and I’ll be discussing that at the bottom of the program. But before either my dialogue with Jessica Tarlov or the book discussion of Yesteryear , I wanna open with some thoughts about an outrage that happened in a place very close to me, just this, these past days. On the Jewish holiday of Yom Kippur, the most holy day of the Jewish year, a gunman opened fire on the synagogue in this Canadian town, the Ontario town of Belleville. Many of the details of this incident remain a little murky, but what we do have is: The alleged gunman, the apparent gunman, is in hospital, and so is a police officer who gallantly came to the rescue of the synagogue. None of the worshippers in the synagogue were injured. The alleged gunman apparently used a shotgun, which discharged a lot of pellets, did a lot of physical damage, but it was not the kind of high-powered rifle that would’ve shot up this building. And so the people inside were safe. This story has become a big story in Ontario, in Canada, and around the world. It is one of a many of a long series of incidents of intensifying violence against Jewish worshippers all around the world since October 7th of 2023. To read about it in Belleville is very striking, however, and not just because it’s so close to me. I have worshipped at the synagogue, Sons of Jacob Synagogue, where the crime took place. I’ve spent a lot of time there. It’s near where I live in Ontario. I see this street in my mind, and it’s such a powerful symbol of how life has changed for North American Jews. The Sons of Jacob Synagogue is a congregation that dates back to the early 20th century, but the building was built in the middle 1950s. It’s a piece of modernist architecture, quite small, and it faces directly on a road in a residential neighborhood. There are no security precautions other than a locked door, because it was built at a time when it never occurred to the Jews of North America that they could face violence from their neighbors. That kind of threat was something they remembered, but from across the ocean and from a different time, not here and not now. But, of course, it is here, and it is now. And it is striking all over the continent, all over the world. When these kinds of incidents happen, a certain kind of speaker, a certain kind of politician, a certain kind of online influencer, a certain kind of journalist will say, It is very important not to conflate the Jews of here— wherever “here” is, Ontario and Canada, the United States, New York, wherever it is— with the Jews over there. We should not be blaming the Jews of Belleville for the crimes of the state of Israel. Now this kind of remark is intended to be a defense of the Jewish community that is under attack, but it is, in its own way, a form of incitement. Because when you say we must not conflate the Jews here with the Jews there, we must not blame our Jews for those Jews, what you’re doing is suggesting that there are some Jews who deserve the kind of violence just that happened. And what you’re also doing is offering safety to certain Jews on condition that they disavow others. We see a lot of this in remarks by some people who are disaffiliated Jews, who will say, We can be safer if only we separate ourselves from the Jews in Israel who are under attack. We can buy some safety for ourselves. I hear that, and I think that that is the counsel of cowardice. To buy safety for yourself by abandoning others, by separating yourself from others who equally deserve safety, that seems to me a reprehensible thing. But as a strictly factual matter, it’s just wrong. That the no-conflation argument— Don’t attack the Jews here for what the Jews over there did —begins with the foundation upon a lie. And the lie is the lie that we are hearing again and again that Israel committed genocide, that is, Nazi-like atrocities, in its war of self-defense that began when it was attacked so atrociously on October 7th, 2023. I once made it a project to dig back through the archives to find who was the first person who compared the state of Israel to the Nazis, and when did it happen? And as best I can tell, the first, or the first prominent person, to do it was the British historian Arnold Toynbee, who makes the point in a book published in 1954, the eighth volume of his Study of History. Within six years of the independence of the state of Israel, Arnold Toynbee is publishing a comparison of the state of Israel to the Nazis. Now, what makes the comparison extra piquant is that Arnold Toynbee was pretty Nazi-adjacent himself. He had been invited to meet with Adolf Hitler in 1936. He took the meeting, and he came back from the meeting praising Hitler’s good intentions and recommending that the British government find a way to learn to live in peace with Adolf Hitler, who wanted nothing more than a better deal for Germany and Europe. So the tradition is Israel is accused of being a Nazi state from the very beginning, by someone who is kind of Nazi-adjacent. And this is a pattern that I think many people who are involved in Jewish life have noticed never ceasing to stop. Because for so many people, what a convenience, what a mercy, what a gift it would be if only we could prove that the Jews were the real Nazis. What a relief. What a burden discharged. There’s a joke, I’m sure you’ve heard it, that the Germans will never forgive the Jews for Auschwitz. I’m happy to report in the modern state of Germany, which is a state that is, in fact, where friendship with Israel is a principle of the organization of the state, the Germans have forgiven the Jews for Auschwitz. But around the rest of the world, lots of people haven’t. Auschwitz is the ultimate nightmare reflection of modern civilization, and specifically of Western civilization and of the Christian culture on which that Western civilization was built. Auschwitz invites a burden of reflection and of guilt that understandably people chafe at. And the way to escape that burden of guilt for many people is to transfer it and to say, The people who are victims there, they deserved it in some way. They’re the culprits, or they deserve it now. Maybe they didn’t deserve it then, but they deserve it now. And so while Germany has forgiven the Jews for Auschwitz, the rest of the world is angrier than ever at the Jews for Auschwitz and so wants to make Auschwitz not just a thing the Jews suffered, but a thing the Jews did. And sad to report, there are Jews or people of Jewish origin who play this game by identifying themselves with the Jewish people and the Jewish community only in order to act as fellow accusers of the Jewish community and the Jewish people. A Democratic nominee for Congress, Brad Lander, who did an event on Yom Kippur where he accused the Jews of the state of Israel of genocide, and a man who’s always separated himself from the state of Israel when the state of Israel was in need, but is rushing to identify himself with the state of Israel when he can blame the state of Israel for Nazi-like crimes. In Canada, the place where the Belleville shooting took place, the leader of the small left-wing party, the New Democratic Party, is of Jewish origin, from a famous Jewish political dynasty in Canada. He opened the Yom Kippur holiday by again saying, as someone who separated himself from Israel always in its time of need, I will identify with Israel to accuse Israel . It’s a footnote to history here that I sometimes think about. The phrase blood libel refers to a myth that the Jews use blood in the making of matzah. And as far as historians can tell, the myth originated in England in the 1100s, when a boy disappeared and a local mob became convinced or was persuaded that the boy had been abducted by the local Jewish community and his blood used to make matzah, and then massacres then followed. This outrageously false accusation was recorded in a book written by a local monk who claimed to have been told that Jews did this by a man named Theobald of Cambridge, a converted Jew who revealed the secrets of the Jewish world, among them that Jews met once a year to pick a Christian child and condemn that child to death for his blood to be used in the making of matzah. Now, it’s not clear whether Theobald of Cambridge actually existed, or whether the monk who told the story invented him or distorted his words in some way. The history of Theobald of Cambridge is a little murky. I like to believe that he did exist. I like to believe that Theo—I like to imagine Theobald of Cambridge saying in the 1100s, As a Jew, I’m here to tell you that the Jews really do use blood in the making of matzah, and you’re right to go out and massacre them all to punish them for the crime I just invented to defame my own community. And what I want to say when I hear people saying, As a Jew, I accuse the Jews of being Nazis, is—we had one Theobald of Cambridge already. He did enough damage. We don’t need more. But the modern progressive left, whether its members are of Jewish origin or not, tends to identify the Jews as privileged and powerful, and therefore as dangerous. And they often will see the Holocaust itself not as a source of suffering and misery, of trauma, which continues to affect Jewish mentality and Jewish life all these years after it happened; they see the Holocaust as a source of Jewish power and privilege, and therefore something that needs to be redistributed from the Jews to someone who is more deserving, who needs their share of power and privilege, and the kind of power and privilege you get by having a Holocaust of your own. And that is what is going on with this conflation lie. The conflation to say, We are going to accuse the Jews of the very thing that was done to them. Of the thing that was done to them not only in the 1940s, but of the thing that was attempted against them on October 7th, 2023, when there was a Nazi-like atrocity against the Jews of Israel—mass murder, mass kidnapping, mass rape, mass torture. That was how this war started. And so to redistribute the odium for those offenses, we redistribute it to those who need to have the history of the Holocaust redistributed away from them. And that brings us to the shooting in Belleville. And whenever I make these points, which are very close to my heart, I’m asked the question, Well, are you saying that all criticism of the state of Israel must be anti-Semitic? Can’t somebody say things about the Jews and not be anti-Semitic? And obviously, that’s true. People do it all the time, including many Israelis. Israelis criticize their own state. But If you say, I want to criticize the Jews without being regarded as anti-Semitic, one of the great ways of criticizing the state of Israel without being anti-Semitic is not to be anti-Semitic. It’s not so hard. Not to have paranoid fantasies. Not to engage in ancient anti-Semitic tropes, not to deploy myths of Jewish conspiracy and secret power and privilege. Not, above all, to say, We are going to accuse the Jews of doing the thing that was done to them, because they don’t deserve the credit for it, and someone else needs it as a resource for their power and privilege. That is the path to the shooting in Belleville, Ontario, and to so many other crimes that we are seeing and suffering in our modern world. And now, my dialogue with Jessica Tarlov. [ Music ] Frum: If you’ve ever caught the program The Five on Fox News, and who hasn’t, you know exactly what Jessica Tarlov does for a living. She regularly sits down at a table with four people who disagree with her, and she does not flinch. And I’m not. I enjoy the dynamic of the table at The Five , and the relationships and the rapport that I have with these colleagues, and the way that I’m able to talk about these issues in a long-term sense. And I think that that’s a much more realistic way to be having these conversations with people who are ideologically different, than to sit down for a one-off couple-hour conversation with someone who has a lot of views that you might find really repellent. Frum: One of the themes I hear in your answer is: You have this powerful and admirable trust in the reach of reason. If you can seem reasonable, if you can use reason, you can make an influence. I often find myself as I get older wondering how much human beings are reasonable creatures, and whether reason is what moves them. And a story here, when you talk about being with 20 to one. I was in a situation a long time ago at the beginning of the Iraq War. I’d gone to London to watch the debate in the House of Commons about whether Britain should enter the Iraq War. And there was a big march, and I wanted to watch the march. So I changed out of my House of Parliament clothes into ordinary street clothes, and just counted on being obscure enough that I could join the march, and I was in Trafalgar Square. But somebody recognized me from one of the TV shows, and a quite large and quite hostile crowd gathered around me. It was quite aggressive. And it was getting, it was getting a little testy. And so I … after a few minutes of sort of people yelling at me and me yelling back, it became clear they were not going to let me escape so easily. That there might actually be, you know, a little punch thrown. So I stood on the lip of the fountain in Trafalgar Square and said to the group of people—there were now probably about 40 of them —I’ll tell you what, I will stand here for exactly 20 minutes . Or whatever the figure was; 30, 20, 30. And answer whatever questions you have, and about President Bush and what I know about Prime Minister Blair, and then I’m going to leave. And I did it. And as I spoke to them, they did become calmer. And when the time came, the appointed time came, they did part and let me go without any altercation. And at the time, I thought what I’d done was I had shown the power of reason. But in retrospect, I look back and just say—what I’d done was, I sort of escalated the confrontation. Said, you know, If you want to turn mob violence on me, you’re obviously going to win. But I’m going to give an account of myself. And just somehow there was a kind of subrational communication, that meant that we could talk for 20 or 30 minutes or whatever it was. And then they parted and let me go, which they were not going to do if I hadn’t engaged with them in the first place. And I think about that story. And what did I learn about my fellow human creatures there and the power of reason, or the non-power of reason? Tarlov: That’s a great story also. And I’m not sure that I would’ve thought to do that. So good quick thinking at that moment, because I know how tense it was. But I think that that story is about what we were talking about earlier on in this conversation. Not necessarily reason, or not reason, or the ability to tap into someone’s rationality. But this universal desire to communicate, and to be heard and recognized as having a set of beliefs or a perspective worth your time. And that’s what you told them. You said: What you think and what you believe right now matters, and it matters to me. And yes; you gave an allotment of time and said, It doesn’t matter to me for more than 30 minutes. But 30 minutes when you don’t really know what’s about to happen does feel like a good, you know, chunk of change there. So that’s what I heard in that story. But you recognized their humanity and the universal desire that we all have to be taken seriously and as rational actors, right? With a point of view worth tangoing with. And that is very much what I’m talking about in I Disagree, and that a lot of relationships can be resuscitated or built from focusing on exactly what you did. Which is: You’ve got something to get off your chest. Likewise, I’ve got something to get off my chest. Let’s find a way to do this. Frum: Let me ask you one last question, with something you said a minute ago. You talked about how many of the people with crazy views are very good debaters. And that’s clearly true. And in fact, one of the reasons I have pause with the whole concept of “debate” is: I guarantee that if any normal person debates an anti-vaxxer, the normal person will lose. And the reason that the normal person will lose is because if you’re a normal person, you have a beautiful new baby; you go to the doctor and say, What shot should I give the baby? The doctor says, You should have this schedule of shots, and you do it. And you don’t ask too many questions why, because you’re not a nut. But the nut goes and spends two hours researching vaccines on the internet, which is not enough time to understand anything in a way that a scientist gives his life or her life to understand it. But the nut gives 10, 20, 30 hours; certainly enough to overwhelm the normal person. When you step onto an airplane, how does the jet work? You don’t know. I mean, vaguely, maybe you remember something from a book you read once or Popular Mechanics, but you don’t really know. Someone who believes that jet engines don’t fly would overwhelm you in argument. Only, they do fly. And then the project of debating “the jet engines don’t work,” “vaccines aren’t real” becomes kind of a doomed undertaking. Because the crank knows not-enough, but knows more than you. Tarlov: Yes, and feels more passionately about it, or that you have to defend it at that level. I find that parsing the crazy helps a lot. And I write about this in the book—the importance in engaging as much as you can. And again, this is my job, right? This isn’t purely for fun. So obviously that’s a factor in this, and I want that out there. But spending the time to understand what is going on within the anti-vax movement. Or I think more generally or more appropriately, we need to spend time understanding the MAHA movement, which this is a dangerous facet of. But I happen to have friends who are very smart and rational people who were very interested and had been talking about a lot of the things that RFK Jr. was discussing, vis-à-vis the dyes in our food, and what this was doing to kids. And I’m not a good-enough mom that I have stopped all macaroni-and-cheese intake. But those aren’t a bunch of crazy people. Those are people who are doing the vaccine schedule, absolutely everything the doctor tells you to do—but are also saying, like, the impact of Big Food, or whatever we’re supposed to call it, is completely damaging to all of us, and especially our kid. They’re concerned about microplastics, all of this. And this is how you have these strange bedfellows, politically speaking. And so I do think tussling with that is worthwhile, because at least you can call the balls and strikes within it. Like, I went through the “Big Beautiful Bill” to see where the good points were, because Lisa Murkowski, for instance, is someone who I think is a rational actor. I think that she is a moral, good person. You can’t say you’re one of six that voted to convict Trump after the January 6th insurrection and have spoken out against a lot of the enormous overreaches of this government, and Donald Trump personally, and she found a way to yes . So what is in this bill that is at least decent? And so I guess that would be my response about someone who is an anti-vaxxer. You know, to talk to parents who do exist that think that the schedule has gotten too full, and that we have—it’s too close together. It’s too much for little kids. I mean, I go to a very, like, liberal pediatrician. You know, downtown Manhattan. And they talk to us about the vaccine schedule, and whether we wanted to go at their recommended one, or these were the shots where the option was to split it up. Like, do you want to do this, and then come back a week later? Sometimes that’s all people want to hear, and it gets lumped into this anti-vax sentiment. And it’s questions around what a baby can take at that moment. Now there, of course, there’s the bullshit components of it. About, you know, that we’re just adding vaccines willy-nilly, and we objectively don’t need these things—and we know that is not true. But engaging with their arguments, and spending time with it outside of the bounds of debating with them live, but for your own personal education, I think is very valuable. Frum: Well, let me tell one more anecdote that sort of would be my counter to engaging with the vaccine schedule. This is probably before you became very politically aware, but 1992—this is before 9/11—1992, the election of Bill Clinton. And [George] H. W. Bush on running for reelection, and Ross Perot. There were a series of debates, and the last was a town hall moderated by Carole Simpson of ABC. And people stood up and asked questions of the three candidates. And this is the political story I think about maybe more than any other. So one of the people who stood up to ask a question was an older woman who was obviously very nervous about being on TV the one and only time in her life, in front of tens of millions of Americans. And she asked, I would like to ask each of the candidates how you personally have been affected by the deficit. President George H. W. Bush unfortunately has to go first, and he tries to explain interest rates, and it doesn’t work. And then Ross Perot goes second, and he says something characteristically insane. And then it’s Bill Clinton’s turn, and he moves that giant body of his as close to the woman as the setup will allow. And he answers, I will answer your question, but before I do, let me ask you a question. How have you personally been affected by the deficit? And as she spoke, it became clear that—either because she was nervous and got confused, or maybe she’d never known the difference in the first place—she didn’t mean the deficit. She meant the recession that was also happening at the same time. She’d mixed them up. She wasn’t speaking her native language of human beings. She was speaking political speak, or economic speak. And once Bill Clinton understood the real question, well, he hit it out of the park. I’m the governor of a small state. If people lose their jobs, I probably know them or know their families. Bango. And that was the moment that came to be known as the “I feel your pain” moment, although Bill Clinton never literally said that. And one of the things I learned from that is: You have to hear the question behind the question. So when I hear a mother of a precious newborn talking about the vaccine schedule, I mean, you can engage with that and say, Look, this is crazy. This idea that the vaccines are too close together, no reputable scientist would give that even two minutes of attention. But if I engage with you on that, I’m actually not only not helping the discussion, I’m not helping you—because I’m not talking about what you really care about. Which is: You’ve brought this beautiful creature into an uncertain world, and you’re full of fears. And your fears have latched onto something they shouldn’t latch onto, which is the vaccine schedule, where you just do what the pediatrician says and not ask questions. But you have these other fears, and they are deeper, and maybe we can address them. But understanding that you may not yourself understand why you are saying the things you say. And if I answer the things you say, I’m not serving either myself or you. Tarlov: So I think there is a way to do both. I totally agree with you about the underlying issue, which is that you’re afraid because you have this incredible precious cargo now, and the idea that they’re going to get pricked. But I think that you can do both things to say, I can sense that you’re afraid and that you don’t want your little baby boy or your little baby girl to be in any pain. But I do think that it is incumbent upon us to talk to people about what they think, and where they are getting that information. And then to find a way to say, But the science says, without seeming like a total jerk, and that we’re not particularly good at that. This is what has happened to a large degree in the debate about climate change, for instance. You notice how even people like Bill Gates, who were out front in terms of talking about the deleterious impacts of climate change and rising sea levels and temperatures and all of it, has even backtracked somewhat on what he said was going to happen. And obviously there was tons of hyperbole around it from electeds, and even people in the scientific community. All of that wears on people, and I don’t think that it is worthwhile. It’s one thing to be dismissive of having a conversation with the king vax crank—so like RFK Jr., pre-HHS secretary—so, you know, before he was somehow responsible for all of us. Which is a travesty. But the person who is following along, or who has this different kind of source material than you, I don’t think it should be beneath us to engage in that. Because again, if you take them seriously and you show them and their views some level of respect, it makes room for them to hear a counter opinion. And I’m not saying, again, that you’re going to necessarily change their mind. But you might open it up to the idea that perhaps more research should be done. And that’s how you get these moments, right? All of these people who say like, Oh my God, and then I realized X, Y, or Z thing wasn’t reality. Or, He wasn’t really on my side. So all of these Trump voters right now that are having regrets about it. And if you don’t make a gentler space for that to happen, that’s where you really lose people. And then they have no interest in even talking to you, let alone listening to a program that we might host. Frum: Jessica, you are so good at what you do. Thank you for joining me today on The David Frum Show . I’m so grateful to you. Tarlov: Oh, it was fabulous. Thank you for having me. Frum: Bye-bye. [ Music ] Frum: Thanks so much to Jessica Tarlov for joining me today on The David Frum Show. As I mentioned at the top of the show, my book this week is a novel: Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke. I sometimes think if I ever had to teach writing, and I hope I never will, but if I ever had to, I would want to assign my students novels that were almost good. How much, after all, are any of us going to learn from reading Ulysses or Remembrance of Things Past ? Those are works of unique genius, and we’re not going to ever manage to achieve anything like that. But we can write better books, and the way to write better books is by looking at books that are pretty good but not quite there and trying to figure out what went wrong. Yesteryear is a novel that has been a big commercial success. Much praise; it’s in book clubs. It’s been profiled on television. And indeed, it is very clever and engaging. I enjoyed reading it. It is the story of an online influencer who leads the life of a tradwife and is very commercially successful. Sells products, has millions of followers on Instagram. Who is, by some trick of—well, I won’t go too much into the trick, because this is the hinge on which the novel turns, but is catapulted back into the past and finds herself on a farm that looks very like her own farm with a family that looks very like her own family. Only in the year 1855, where the the trad in traditional becomes a little more sinister. I think a lot of people have this fantasy about what it would be like to go back into past, but they never think what would it be like to not have dentistry, to not have antibiotics, to not know why chickens and cows get sick. And of course, to be completely isolated in the country without roads, without cars, without any access to the outside world. So that’s a very ingenious gimmick, and it’s won the novel a lot of attention. And apparently the novel has been optioned for the movies, and I’m sure it will make a fine movie. And as a novel, it’s entertaining, amusing, interesting, provocative. But it’s not quite a good piece of writing. And it’s worth, I think, some time to think about why not. Why does it just fail? And what is the consequence of that just failure? To my mind, the difference between good and almost good is we can enjoy an almost-good novel in the here and now. We can enjoy its cleverness. We can enjoy its satire. We can enjoy its reflections on contemporary society. And then it will be forgotten, and 10 years from now, 15, no one will return to it. Books that are good are famously described as “news that stays news.” Yesteryear won’t stay news, and here’s why. The first problem, and the least of the problems, is the way the book is written. Yesteryear is constructed as a first-person narrative. The central character is also the person who tells the story. So anytime the writer wants to write, the writer has to remember that she’s writing in the voice of her principal character. Well, Caro Claire Burke loves to write. There’s writing all over this book, and what she especially loves are similes and metaphors. Again and again, a thing is compared to another thing. At one point, the sound of a camera clicking is compared to the closing of a prison gate. A depressed woman who is slumping a little bit in her chair is compared to shriveled fruit. A gloomy face is compared to a lunar eclipse. People left behind in a room after a more powerful person has exited the room are compared to fallen puppets. And so it goes. I mean, there’s one of those on every page. Obviously, the writer enjoys them and admires them and thinks they’re very clever. And some are okay; some are less good. But the question she doesn’t stop to ask is: Would her narrator, in fact, talk like that, and talk like that all the time? So in order to advance her own idea of writing, she is losing her connection to her character. The second and more important strike to the book is a lack of object permanence. Why do things happen? People have different relationships to each other on one page of the book than they have later, as the author’s satirical purposes require and her polemical purposes require. The author has very strong points of view, so every once in a while she needs to slap somebody she doesn’t like. And then things happen that are in no way indicated or built up to by any previous buildup, or any previous characterization. Finally, there is a kind of lack of sympathy through the book. Now, there’s nothing wrong with having an unsympathetic principal character. Thackeray did it in Vanity Fair. But Becky Sharp, although she’s not a very likable or admirable character, she’s a fascinating character. She’s someone we inhabit from within, and she’s not a completely horrible-in-every-way character. She has certain excellences and attributes, and so do some the people around her. We feel sympathy for her victims, because many of them are nicer people than she is. If you hate everybody and make everybody the butt of your humor and your satire and your polemical points, then we end up living as if we were this unlikable narrator. One of the questions that fans who praise the book will say is, You have to understand; you have to enter into the spirit of the book. And the spirit of the book is “the main character’s nasty, so everybody in the book is nasty”—and that’s the author’s art. But you’re left wondering after a while, maybe it’s not just the characters who are nasty, principal and secondary; maybe the author’s kind of nasty. I’m not sure—I mean, she’s clever, and she’s got funny things to say. I’m not sure I’m enjoying spending time with her and not just with her character. But the book is famous. I’m sure you’ll have a chance to read it for yourself. See if you agree or disagree with me. That’s it for this week’s edition of The David Frum Show. Thanks so much for watching or listening. As always, the best way to support the work of this program is by subscribing to The Atlantic. That way, you get my work and all of my colleagues’. I hope you will consider sharing and promoting the program on whatever social-media platform you use. See you next week here on The David Frum Show. Bye-bye.

items.title: Mahama urges global institutions to invest in Africa’s cultural infrastructure
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has called on multilateral development banks, international financial institutions, global foundations and private sector partners to invest in Africa’s cultural infrastructure. He said greater investment was needed to strengthen the continent’s ability to preserve, research and showcase its cultural heritage, particularly as efforts intensify to secure the restitution of African artefacts held abroad. Speaking at a High-Level Side Event on the Next Steps on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, President Mahama said cultural heritage should be treated as an important component of Africa’s development. “Today, I make a direct call to multilateral development banks, international financial institutions, global foundations, and private sector partners: Invest deliberately in Africa’s cultural infrastructure,” he siad. He urged development partners to channel financing into regional archives, conservation laboratories and digitisation initiatives, as well as professional training for a new generation of African curators and historians. According to President Mahama, investment in cultural infrastructure would help African countries effectively receive, preserve and manage artefacts and other heritage materials returned to the continent. His call forms part of Ghana’s broader reparatory justice agenda, which seeks to move beyond acknowledgement of historical injustices towards practical measures, including the restitution of African cultural property.

items.title: Souveraineté énergétique : le Sénégal prépare une deuxième raffinerie de 4 millions de tonnes
items.description: En marge de la 81e session de l’Assemblée générale des Nations unies, le président de la République, Bassirou Diomaye Diakhar Faye, a présidé, mercredi 23 septembre 2026, à New York, la cérémonie de signature d’un protocole d’accord entre la Société africaine de raffinage (SAR) et la compagnie turque Yamata. Cet accord ouvre la voie à un vaste programme visant à renforcer les capacités de raffinage et à accélérer la marche du Sénégal vers la souveraineté énergétique. Le document a été signé par le directeur général de la SAR, Mamadou Abib Diop, et le président-directeur général de Yamata, Cengiz Duyar. Il prévoit notamment la construction d’une deuxième raffinerie d’une capacité de quatre millions de tonnes par an. L’installation sera conçue pour traiter le pétrole brut de Sangomar, mais également une large gamme de bruts disponibles sur le marché international. Un investissement pouvant atteindre 3 milliards de dollars Le coût de cette nouvelle infrastructure est estimé entre 2 et 3 milliards de dollars. Le partenariat prévoit également la modernisation de la raffinerie de Mbao, actuellement en activité, pour un investissement supplémentaire compris entre 300 et 500 millions de dollars. Yamata devra assurer l’ingénierie, les achats, la construction ainsi que le financement du projet. La compagnie turque entend mobiliser les ressources nécessaires auprès de ses partenaires financiers, sans garantie souveraine de l’État du Sénégal. La signature du protocole marque ainsi une nouvelle étape dans le processus. Elle doit permettre de finaliser les études d’ingénierie de détail, présentées comme la dernière phase avant le démarrage de la construction. Couvrir les besoins nationaux et viser le marché régional Depuis le démarrage de sa production pétrolière en 2024, le Sénégal demeure encore largement dépendant des importations de produits pétroliers. La mise en service d’une nouvelle raffinerie doit contribuer à réduire cette dépendance. Selon la présidence de la République, la future installation aura vocation à couvrir l’intégralité des besoins du marché national et à dégager des excédents destinés aux marchés de la sous-région. Le projet s’inscrit ainsi dans une ambition plus large : faire évoluer le Sénégal d’un producteur de pétrole brut vers un pays capable de transformer une partie significative de sa production et de devenir un fournisseur régional de produits raffinés. Des perspectives au-delà du raffinage L’enjeu du projet dépasse toutefois la seule production de carburants. Une capacité de raffinage accrue doit également permettre de fournir des intrants à plusieurs secteurs de l’économie, notamment l’agriculture, les transports, l’industrie et la construction. Le partenariat prévoit par ailleurs le développement de projets connexes dans la pétrochimie. L’objectif est de favoriser la transformation locale des dérivés du pétrole et de faire émerger de nouvelles chaînes de valeur industrielles. La présidence présente ainsi cette initiative comme un projet à effet catalytique, susceptible de stimuler les investissements, le développement des compétences et la participation des entreprises sénégalaises dans plusieurs secteurs. Plus de 15 000 emplois annoncés Le projet devrait générer plus de 15 000 emplois directs durant sa phase de construction, avec une place importante accordée au contenu local. Les métiers liés à l’ingénierie, à la maintenance et à la logistique industrielle figurent notamment parmi les domaines appelés à bénéficier de cette dynamique. À travers ce partenariat, le chef de l’État réaffirme ainsi l’objectif de renforcer la souveraineté énergétique du Sénégal. Pour les autorités, le recours à un financement privé, sans garantie souveraine, doit permettre de porter ce programme d’investissement sans alourdir directement les finances publiques. C.G. DIOP

items.title: Kuami Eugene joins UNICEF Ghana to promote universal birth registration
items.description: Multiple award-winning Ghanaian musician Kuami Eugene has joined a UNICEF Ghana-led advocacy campaign in Bepoasi in the Eastern Region, aimed at promoting universal birth registration and ensuring that no child is left without an official record of birth. The initiative took the musician and a UNICEF Ghana delegation, led by its new Representative, Andy Brooks, to the remote farming community, where residents participated in a registration exercise and a community durbar focused on the importance of birth registration. Bepoasi, located in the Ayensuanu District, is home to more than 3,000 people, many of whom are engaged in farming. For children born without official birth records, the consequences can extend far beyond the absence of a document. A lack of registration can create barriers to accessing essential services and exercising basic rights, including education and other public services. Speaking during the visit, UNICEF Ghana and its partners underscored the need for universal birth registration as a critical part of ensuring that every child is formally recognised and accounted for. The UNICEF Ghana-led team received a warm welcome from residents, with Kuami Eugene’s presence adding excitement to the registration exercise and community durbar. The musician, who enjoys a strong following among Ghanaian music fans, used the platform to support the call for parents and communities to prioritise the registration of children at birth. A representative of the Births and Deaths Registry, Edward Abrahams, also highlighted the long-term importance of the exercise and called for sustained support to extend birth registration services to communities across the country. The campaign forms part of broader efforts to ensure that children are not left without the legal identity and documentation needed to access essential services and opportunities. The message from the community engagement was clear: an unregistered child risks becoming an invisible child. UNICEF Ghana and its partners are therefore urging parents, caregivers and communities to register every child at birth and help ensure that every child in Ghana has an official identity from the very beginning of life.

items.title: Renard warns Côte d’Ivoire against complacency Ahead of Ghana clash
items.description: Côte d’Ivoire head coach Hervé Renard has urged his players to remain humble as they prepare to face Ghana in their opening 2027 Africa Cup of Nations qualifying fixture. The Elephants head into the clash with confidence, but Renard is aware of the threat posed by the Black Stars, despite Ghana suffering injuries to several key players, including captain Jordan Ayew, Mohammed Kudus and Antoine Semenyo. Renard believes his team has the character to secure a positive result but insists that quality must be demonstrated on the pitch. “When you have a match between two big teams, it will be played on details. But we have enough character to approach it. It is not enough to say it; it will have to be shown on the pitch,” he said. The French coach also cautioned his players against looking beyond their opening fixture, stressing that the qualification campaign will be decided over six matches. “There are six matches to be played. Sometimes we miss the first step and pass the others. You have to be humble,” Renard added.

items.title: ‘Can the patient feel the difference?’ – GMTF boss challenges health leaders
items.description: Administrator for the Ghana Medical Trust Fund (GMTF), Adjoa Obuobia Darko-Opoku, has challenged nursing and midwifery leaders to ensure that health policies and strategies translate into tangible improvements in the experience of patients. She said the success of leadership in the health sector should not be measured only by policies developed or strategies adopted, but by whether patients actually experience better care when they walk into a health facility. “The patient does not experience our policy documents. The patient experiences the system,” she said, stressing the need for health leaders to bridge the gap between policy decisions and what happens at the point of care. Speaking at a conference of Senior Nursing and Midwifery Managers, Mrs Darko-Opoku urged nursing and midwifery leaders to demonstrate competence, compassion, mentorship and courage in their daily work. She cautioned against allowing poor communication, unnecessary delays and malfunctioning equipment to become accepted features of healthcare delivery. She said frontline health workers play a critical role in shaping the culture of healthcare institutions because their decisions and conduct directly influence patients’ experiences. According to her, leadership must therefore be intentional about identifying problems, addressing them and setting standards that improve service delivery. Mrs Darko-Opoku also called for stronger representation of nursing and midwifery professionals in health policy discussions, arguing that the practical knowledge gained at the frontline must inform decisions taken at the highest levels of the health system. She said nurses and midwives who interact directly with patients have valuable insights into the challenges within healthcare facilities and should have a meaningful voice in designing policies intended to address those challenges. “Small leadership decisions, repeated consistently, become institutional culture and institutional culture eventually becomes the health system,” she said, urging health managers to recognise the long-term impact of their everyday decisions. Mrs Darko-Opoku challenged health leaders to make their work visible through the quality of care patients receive, rather than through policies and strategies alone. She urged them to make leadership personal, professionalism visible and, above all, ensure that every patient can genuinely feel the difference their leadership makes.

items.title: AFCON qualifiers: Nigeria vs Madagascar – date, time, venue and where to watch
items.description: By Adegboyega Adeleye The Super Eagles of Nigeria will begin their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, AFCON qualifying campaign when they host Madagascar at the Godswill Akpabio International Stadium, Uyo, on Friday. Eric Chelle’s side will be aiming for a winning start in Group L as they begin their bid to qualify for the tournament, which will be co-hosted by Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda. The Super Eagles head into the clash after a mixed run in their recent international fixtures, having defeated Zimbabwe and Jamaica before drawing with Poland and losing 2-1 to Portugal in June. The defeat to Portugal ended Nigeria’s 12-match unbeaten run under Chelle and was their first loss in regulation time since the Malian took charge. Chelle will, however, have to plan without Victor Osimhen after the Galatasaray striker was ruled out of Nigeria’s first two qualifiers with a right adductor strain. Taiwo Awoniyi has been recalled as his replacement, while Akor Adams, Tolu Arokodare and George Ilenikhena are among the other attacking options available to the coach. Ademola Lookman, Moses Simon and Samuel Chukwueze are also expected to provide attacking options as Nigeria begin their qualification campaign. Madagascar will arrive in Uyo with a 25-man squad led by captain Rayan Raveloson, while coach Corentin Martins has handed first international call-ups to striker Roman Ferber and goalkeeper Zacharie Boucher. The Barea will also be looking to draw confidence from their previous meeting with Nigeria after securing a memorable 2-0 victory over the Super Eagles at the 2019 Africa Cup of Nations in Egypt. Nigeria have won three of their five previous meetings with Madagascar, while one ended in a draw and the Barea have recorded one victory. However, the three-time African champions will be seeking to start this qualifying campaign on a stronger note, with only one qualification place available from Group L because Tanzania have already secured their place as co-hosts. Following Friday’s encounter, Nigeria will travel to Guinea-Bissau for their second Group L fixture on September 29. Date, time and venue The 2027 AFCON qualifying match between Nigeria and Madagascar will be played on Friday, September 25, at the Godswill Akpabio International Stadium in Uyo. Kick-off is scheduled for 5:00 p.m. Nigerian time (4:00 p.m. GMT). Where to watch The match will be available to fans through the official broadcast and streaming platforms holding the rights to the 2027 AFCON qualifiers. Viewers are advised to check local listings and official broadcaster platforms for the confirmed transmission details ahead of kick-off. items.title: Batna : ignoré par ses proches, un jeune marié trouve toute l’Algérie à ses côtés
items.description: L'histoire est triste et merveilleuse à la fois. Triste, parce qu’un jeune orphelin s’est retrouvé presque seul lors de son mariage , ses proches n’ayant pas daigné faire le déplacement. Mais la fin est heureuse. Les habitants de sa ville et de toutes les régions du pays lui ont organisé une fête grandiose. C’est un cas de solidarité collective insolite et émouvant. Laissé seul le jour de son mariage, il reçoit une foule immense L’histoire s’est passée à Merouana, une localité de la wilaya de Batna, dans l’Est de l’Algérie. Salah, un jeune orphelin, a organisé une cérémonie pour son mariage . Seule une poignée de ses amis était présente. Ses proches n’ont pas répondu à l’invitation. Sur une vidéo partagée sur les réseaux sociaux, on voit le jeune homme abattu, dans une salle presque vide. Les plats préparés pour les invités sont restés intacts. Les internautes ont très vite compris ce qu'il s’est passé. Les invités ne sont pas venus parce que le marié est pauvre et orphelin. Ils sont venus de partout pour lui offrir un mariage de rêve Émus, les jeunes de la région se sont donné le mot pour se retrouver chez lui. L'appel à la solidarité est très vite entendu. Les gens sont venus par centaines. Il y avait même des troupes de cavaliers, du baroud, des véhicules de luxe avec des décorations florales, des motos, des mascottes… La place de la ville est noire de monde, les rues et ruelles bloquées par un nombre impressionnant de voitures. « Même les services de sécurité ont été pris de court et ont eu du mal à réguler la circulation avec le grand nombre de véhicules qui a afflué », raconte un témoin dans une autre vidéo sur les réseaux sociaux. « Hier j’étais tout seul, aujourd'hui 69 wilayas sont avec moi » Sur les images, on voit le marié enfin heureux, s'éclatant avec ses « invités » inattendus. Son mariage est passé du plus triste du monde à une fête dont personne ne peut rêver. Il a eu en tout cas « le plus long cortège du monde », selon l’avis des présents. « Hier j’étais tout seul, aujourd'hui toute l’Algérie, 69 wilayas sont avec moi », déclare Salah. Les gens sont, en effet, venus de Merouana, d’autres localités de Batna et de nombreuses wilayas du pays. Cette histoire fera date. Elle illustre la solidarité séculaire des Algériens. L’article Batna : ignoré par ses proches, un jeune marié trouve toute l’Algérie à ses côtés est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Wael Naouar annonce la suspension de sa grève de la faim après 38 jours
items.description: Wael Naouar a annoncé, dans la soirée de ce mercredi 23 septembre 2026, la suspension de sa grève de la faim après 38 jours d'action protestataire contre son arrestation et celle de ses camarades de la flotille Al-Soumoud. Dans un message adressé à l'opinion publique, l'activiste qui est en détention, explique avoir pris cette décision en réponse aux demandes pressantes de sa famille et de son comité de défense, inquiets de la dégradation critique de son état de santé, ainsi qu'aux appels lancés par diverses organisations nationales, forces politiques et activistes de la société civile. Dans son message, il a adressé un hommage particulier à l'avocat Ayachi Hammami pour son geste de solidarité mené depuis sa cellule, tout en exprimant sa gratitude envers ses proches et l'ensemble de ses soutiens. Par la même occasion, il a appelé ses camarades de la flotille Al-Soumoud arrêtés avec lui, à savoir Ghassen Henchiri, Ghassen Boghdiri et Nabil Chennoufi, à mettre fin eux aussi à leur grève de la faim afin de préserver leur santé et de poursuivre le combat sous d'autres formes. Wael Wael Naouar a par ailleurs souligné que la suspension de ce mouvement de protestation ne constitue en rien un renoncement à ses revendications ou à sa lutte pour la liberté. Y. N. items.title: Kaolack : Le FSDT installe sa structure départementale et annonce 72 heures de grève
items.description: Le Front syndical pour la défense du travail (FSDT) a installé, ce mercredi 23 septembre 2026, a structure départementale à Kaolack. La cérémonie, tenue à la Chambre des métiers, a été mise à profit pour informer les organisations membres sur le nouveau Code du travail, le Pacte de stabilité sociale et le plan d’action réactualisé du mouvement syndical. La rencontre a réuni plusieurs organisations autour des questions d’emploi, de conditions de travail, de protection sociale et de dialogue avec les pouvoirs publics. En marge de la cérémonie, le secrétaire général de la CNTS, Mody Guiro, a invité le ministre de tutelle à privilégier la concertation. « On n’a rien contre le ministre de tutelle lui-même. Mais, à partir de sa fonction, il crée la zizanie. Il l’a même dit : “je vais mettre de l’ordre” », a-t-il déclaré. Estimant que « le dialogue social doit demeurer au cœur » des relations entre autorités et syndicats, Mody Guiro a dénoncé un discours qu’il juge incompatible avec l’esprit de concertation. Dans ce contexte, le FSDT annonce une grève générale de 72 heures, les 21, 22 et 23 octobre 2026, dans les secteurs public, privé et informel. Le mouvement réclame notamment la révision du CDD de quatre ans, l’amélioration de la gouvernance de l’IPRES et de la CSS, l’application de la Convention n°144 de l’OIT, la réintégration de travailleurs licenciés et l’amélioration des conditions salariales et sociales. À Kaolack, le Front entend renforcer son implantation et préparer cette mobilisation prévue en octobre prochain. Mamadou THIAM ( Correspondant)

items.title: Office of the Registrar of Companies marks Risk Awareness Week with push for risk-smart, resilient institution
items.description: The Office of the Registrar of Companies (ORC) has set a new approach to risk management across its directorates and zonal offices, encouraging staff and management to move beyond identifying risk-related issues to actively taking ownership and preventing risk cases at work. The call was made during the official opening of the 2026 Risk Awareness Week on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, under the theme “Building a Risk-Smart ORC: Strengthening Resilience, Accountability and Service Excellence.” The event was held at the ORC conference room in Accra. The four-day programme, scheduled from Tuesday, September 22 to Friday, September 25, 2026, seeks to deepen staff understanding of Enterprise Risk Management (ERM) and strengthen a culture in which risks are identified early, discussed openly and managed or mitigated before they adversely affect the ORC’s operations and service delivery. During the opening ceremony, the Registrar of Companies, Mrs Maame Samma Peprah, Esq., reminded staff that risks associated with ORC’s operations are critical aspects of the institution’s mandate, hence the need to create awareness and take steps to mitigate identified risks. She emphasised that effective risk management cannot be confined to one department or a selected group of staff. Rather, staff across directorates and zonal offices have a role to play in safeguarding the organisation’s resources, reputation and ability to deliver quality services. “The public depends on us for reliable company registration, accurate records, effective compliance services and timely support,” she said. She added that to deliver these services well, staff must recognise the risks that could interrupt their work, weaken public confidence or prevent the institution from achieving its objectives. According to Mrs Peprah, staff should appreciate risk management as a responsibility shared across ORC. She called on directorates, zonal and unit heads as risk owners and risk champions to understand the risks in their areas of work, ensure agreed controls and mitigation measures are carried out, keep risk discussions active, and help identify and report emerging issues. The Registrar indicated the importance of taking risk considerations into everyday decisions and activities, rather than waiting until risks materialise. She said staff should place ownership and accountability firmly at the centre of ORC’s risk management agenda. Mr Prince Kakah, Head of Internal Audit and Risk Coordinator, explained the programme outline for the Risk Awareness Week, saying the Governing Board is determined to incorporate ERM into ORC’s daily operations. He noted that the Board’s focus goes beyond policy documents, aimed at ensuring that risk awareness shapes how staff plan, execute and evaluate their assigned duties at work. Mr Kakah outlined the week’s activities as focusing on promoting awareness and providing practical understanding of risk management to all staff. The activities include Opening and Staff Engagement; Directorate Risk Engagements and Risk Awareness Campaign; Health, Wellness and Organisational Resilience Talk; and a Risk Management Educational Symposium and Awards Ceremony. The final event seeks to recognise and appreciate staff and teams who demonstrate strong risk management practices at the workplace. The opening ceremony brought together the Deputy Registrar of Companies, Mr Benjamin Zigorsh-Nyakpenu, Heads of Directorates, Risk Owners, Risk Champions and other staff of ORC. Heads and staff at the Zonal Offices in Kumasi, Sunyani, Sekondi and Tamale joined virtually, signalling strong institutional support for the ORC risk awareness initiative. It is expected that the 2026 Risk Awareness Week celebration will reinforce the fact that risk management is not merely an audit function, a management responsibility or a compliance requirement, but a collective responsibility for all to be more accountable in taking decisions and better prepared to protect the ORC’s mandate and improve service delivery. The initiative comes as public sector institutions face growing pressure to strengthen governance, accountability and service delivery — areas where the ORC, as the state agency responsible for company registration and compliance, plays a central role in Ghana’s business environment.

Le vote avait débuté à 8h. items.title: Full text: Mahama’s speech at high-level side event on return and restitution of cultural properties and heritage
items.description: Excellencies, Distinguished Colleagues, Ladies and Gentlemen, Imagine, for a moment, Africa before the distant galleries of London, Paris, Berlin, and New York became the main repositories of our history. Imagine a continent where history was not locked behind glass across oceans, but lived among the people. History was carved into sacred wood. Cast in royal bronze. Forged in iron. Woven into Kente. Written in manuscripts. And embodied in sacred objects through which generations remembered who they were. Then imagine those treasures torn from their homes. Seized in punitive expeditions. Stripped from royal compounds. Carried away after conquest. And scattered across the globe. For generations, Africa’s history, memory, and identity have been held far from the hands that created them. This is not a story about static objects in museum cases. It is a story about people. It is a story about dignity. It is a story about an unfinished journey toward justice. Ghana knows this pain intimately. In 1874, British forces destroyed Kumasi, looting the palace of the Asantehene. A century and a half later, in 2024, a portion of that heritage returned, including the sacred Mpomponsuo sword. Its return reminded us that these are not mere relics of a bygone era. They belong to living traditions, active institutions, and communities that are still here. We see this across our continent. We saw it in 1897 in Benin City. We saw it at Maqdala in Ethiopia, and in Abomey in Benin. And we see it in its most heartbreaking form: the removal of the physical remains of our ancestors. In 1838, King Badu Bonsu II of Ahanta rebelled against Dutch colonial domination. The Dutch authorities executed him by hanging and after decapitated him. His head was sent to Netherlands for phrenology studies and was preserved in a jar of formaldehyde for 170 years. Rediscovered by a Dutch journalist in 2002, the head was finally returned to Ghana in 2009. And this is where I say, ladies and genetlemen, Human remains are not collectibles. They are not specimens. They are our ancestors. They are our fathers, mothers, kings, and elders. Restoring them is not a matter of legal ownership; it is a fundamental test of our shared human dignity. Excellencies, on 25th March this year, the UN General Assembly took a historic step. By adopting Resolution 80/250, 123 Member States declared the trafficking of enslaved Africans as the gravest crime against humanity and called for the prompt and unhindered restitution of our cultural property, sacred artefacts, and national archives. That resolution was an indispensable moment of global truth. But truth is not the destination. Truth is the starting line. In June, Ghana convened the High-Level Consultative Conference in Accra. Leaders from Africa, the Caribbean, and around the world gathered to answer one fundamental question: What comes next? Our answer was clear: We must move from acknowledgement to action, from commitments to implementation. The adoption of the Accra Next Steps Commitments on Reparatory Justice provided the blueprint. Today, on the sidelines of the 81st UN General Assembly, I present to you the three pillars of our NEXT STEPS to transform this vision into global reality. First, we acknowledge and salute the progress made. We thank the Netherlands for cataloguing 2,000 Ghanaian artefacts for return. We acknowledge Germany’s engagement with our Kpando traditional area, France’s legislative frameworks, and the return of the Djidji Ayokwe talking drum to Côte d’Ivoire. But moral justice cannot rely on piecemeal generosity or isolated acts of goodwill. Our NEXT STEP is to build a permanent, institutionalised global system. We call on the United Nations and holding nations to establish clear, standardised legal and diplomatic mechanisms that streamline provenance research, make archives transparent, and lower legal barriers to unconditional restitution, starting immediately with the unconditional return of all human remains. Second, too often, we hear the argument that restitution must wait until African nations build modern facilities to secure their heritage. Let us reject this narrative. Capacity constraints must never be used as a justification for continued possession. Capacity must serve as a bridge to return, not a barrier to justice. Africa is already building the infrastructure of the future. Through the African Union’s flagship Agenda 2063 project, we are advancing the Great African Museum. Through the AU-EU Museum Partnership, we are deepening technical collaboration. In Ghana, we are constructing state-of-the-art national and traditional institutions to preserve, research, and exhibit our returning treasures. Where gaps in technology, digitisation, or conservation exist, the solution is simple: Invest in them through genuine multilateral partnership. And third, cultural heritage is not a luxury item to be addressed after economic development. Heritage is an engine of development. Properly preserved and showcased, it fuels education, identity, international tourism, and the booming creative economy. Today, I make a direct call to multilateral development banks, international financial institutions, global foundations, and private sector partners: Invest deliberately in Africa’s cultural infrastructure. We must channel development finance into regional archives, conservation laboratories, digitisation initiatives, and professional training for a new generation of African curators and historians. Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, ultimately, this work is about the children who will inherit our world in Kumasi, Benin City, Addis Ababa, London, Kingston, and New York. When a young African child enters a museum on her own continent and touches the tangible proof of her ancestors’ brilliance, she learns that her history did not begin with subjugation. She learns that her ancestors built empires, mastered metallurgy, engineered complex political systems, and created sublime art. Our young people must inherit more than the story of what Africa lost. They must inherit the story of what Africa created. There is an old Ghanaian proverb that says: “The fact that your child drowned in water does not mean you should never drink water again.” It reminds us that past trauma must not sentence us to permanent estrangement. We cannot rewrite the history of conquest. But we possess the absolute power to write how we heal from it. Ghana does not come to this hall to assign guilt for the past. We come to forge a partnership with the present to repair the future. The story of Africa’s cultural heritage cannot end with its removal. It must continue with its return. Let this UN General Assembly be remembered not as the place where we agreed on the past, but as the moment we built the future together. I thank you.

items.title: ICU urges Ghanaian smock weavers to scale up production for local and export markets
items.description: The General Secretary of the Industrial and Commercial Workers’ Union (ICU), Ghana, Morgan Ayawine, has urged smock weavers and leather workers to prepare for mass production as growing interest in Ghanaian crafts creates new opportunities in local and international markets. He said artisans must move beyond small-scale production and position their businesses to take advantage of the increasing visibility and patronage of smock fabrics and related products. Mr Ayawine made the call in a keynote address at the first national conference of the Ghana Association of Weavers and Leather Workers (GHAWAL) in Wa in the Upper West Region. The conference, held on Thursday, September 10, 2026, at Wa Senior High School, was organised under the theme, “Weaving for Future: Empowering Artisans for National Growth.” Mr Ayawine said smock weaving had historically received less attention than other segments of Ghana’s woven cloth industry, with the fabric’s use and patronage largely associated with the cultural traditions of the five northern regions. He, however, said the craft had gained wider national and international visibility in recent years. “The smock has now assumed an international image and is being increasingly patronised both locally and in many parts of the world. Kudos to President Mahama,” he said. Smock gains wider fashion appeal Mr Ayawine cited a recent fashion display by contestants of TV3’s Ghana’s Most Beautiful as an indication of the changing perception and use of smock fabric. He said the contestants showcased smock material in a range of contemporary designs, including gowns, frocks, skirts, tops and “pata-pata”. “This is clear and compelling evidence that smock material has become fashionable and has attained widespread use and acceptance in Ghana. Indeed, it has become sufficiently popular to be recognised as a form of ‘Wednesday wear’ in Ghana,” he said. He therefore challenged weavers to capitalise on the growing popularity by expanding production of smock fabrics and clothing derivatives for both domestic and export markets. “With your Association now coming into the limelight, you must project yourselves positively and strategically in order to attract investment and Government support towards the formalisation, modernisation and expansion of the smock weaving and related clothing industries,” he said. AGOA offers export opportunity Mr Ayawine also pointed to the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) as a potential pathway for Ghanaian textile products to access international markets. He encouraged GHAWAL to work with the Ghana Export Promotion Authority (GEPA) and other relevant institutions to improve its products and ensure they meet international standards. He said the same approach could be applied to leather and basket products, highlighting the craftsmanship demonstrated in locally made shoes, bags and other leather goods. According to him, achieving greater market access would require deliberate investment in product quality, packaging, branding, marketing and access to finance. He also called for artisans to acquire stronger technical and entrepreneurial skills to enable them to operate more competitive businesses. “As an Association, you must therefore embrace innovation and modern technology without losing the cultural identity and traditional craftsmanship that make your products unique,” he said. ICU pledges support Mr Ayawine assured members that ICU Ghana would provide leadership and support towards projecting the industries and highlighting their contribution to employment, poverty reduction and economic development. He described the conference theme as a call to action and urged artisans to organise effectively, improve quality, embrace innovation and explore new markets. “If you work together with determination, discipline and unity, I have no doubt that your Association will achieve remarkable success,” he said. He further urged participants to make the outcome of the conference practical, forward-looking and focused on measurable results. The conference comes as artisans and producers seek to turn Ghana’s traditional crafts into more commercially viable enterprises. For the smock, leather and basket sectors, improving production capacity, product standards, branding, financing and access to export markets could help artisans move from largely small-scale operations into more formal and competitive businesses. The proposed collaboration with GEPA and use of existing trade opportunities such as AGOA could also provide a framework for artisans and their associations to explore markets beyond Ghana.

items.title: Human remains are not collectibles, specimens – Mahama demands restitution of Africa’s heritage
items.description: President John Dramani Mahama has called for the restitution of African cultural heritage and human remains held in museums and private collections outside the continent. He said the continued possession of African artefacts and the remains of African ancestors was not simply an issue of ownership but one of dignity, identity and justice. Speaking at a High-Level Side Event on the Next Steps on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York, President Mahama said generations of Africans had been separated from important elements of their history and heritage. “Human remains are not collectibles. They are not specimens. They are our ancestors. They are our fathers, mothers, kings, and elders.” He said African heritage had been taken from communities through conquest, punitive expeditions and colonial violence and subsequently dispersed across museums and collections around the world. President Mahama cited the 1874 destruction and looting of the Asante Royal Palace in Kumasi by British forces, noting that some of the heritage taken from Ghana had since been returned, including the Mpomponsuo sword in 2024. He also recounted the case of King Badu Bonsu II of Ahanta, who was executed by Dutch authorities in 1838 and whose head was taken to the Netherlands for phrenological studies. His remains were eventually returned to Ghana in 2009. According to President Mahama, such cases demonstrate why restitution should extend beyond cultural artefacts to the human remains of Africans held abroad. “Restoring them is not a matter of legal ownership; it is a fundamental test of our shared human dignity.” He said African artefacts and remains should be returned to the communities and institutions to which they belong, describing them as part of living traditions rather than relics of a distant past. The President’s call forms part of Ghana’s broader push for reparatory justice, following the adoption of a UN resolution recognising the trafficking and enslavement of Africans and calling for action on the enduring consequences of that history.

items.title: EOCO, Baffour Awuah clash: Article 117 does not give MPs blanket protection from arrest – Samson Ayenini
items.description: Legal practitioner Samson Lardy Anyenini has questioned what he describes as the broad use of parliamentary privilege under Article 117 of Ghana’s 1992 Constitution to prevent the arrest or service of legal processes on Members of Parliament. Speaking on Joy FM’s Top Story on Wednesday, September 23, Mr Anyenini said Article 117 does not provide blanket protection to MPs, but applies when a legislator is “on his way to, attending at or returning from” parliamentary proceedings. The constitutional provision contains that specific qualification. His comments followed a confrontation at the Accra High Court involving Manhyia South MP and lawyer Nana Agyei Baffour Awuah and security personnel reportedly linked to the Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO). Mr Anyenini said the protection had, in his view, been “so abused”, arguing that being an MP should not automatically prevent law enforcement from taking action when Parliament is on recess or when there is no evidence that the legislator is engaged in parliamentary business. He said where an MP claims to have been attending a parliamentary committee proceeding or other official business, that should be capable of verification. “If there is a scheduled committee process in Parliament to which he was to be attending, that is not difficult to prove,” he said, urging EOCO, other interested parties and the media to establish whether such parliamentary business existed at the time of an attempted arrest. Mr Anyenini also referred to Speaker Alban Bagbin’s clarification in 2026 that security agencies do not require his permission before arresting or inviting an MP for questioning. The Speaker said agencies are required to notify his office and provide details of the circumstances and allegations involved. He suggested that law enforcement agencies inviting an MP should copy the Speaker in their correspondence, adding that the Office of the Special Prosecutor follows such an approach. On arrest warrants, Mr Anyenini said a warrant could be obtained where necessary but cautioned against suggesting that one was required in every circumstance, noting that the law gives certain law enforcement officers powers to arrest with or without a warrant. His comments come as competing accounts emerge over Wednesday’s incident. EOCO says it had invited Mr Baffour Awuah twice in February 2026 to assist with an ongoing investigation and later attempted to secure his attendance after the invitations were not honoured. The Office said the attempted arrest was not completed after the situation escalated and officers assessed that further action could endanger public safety. Mr Baffour Awuah, however, has said he was approached after appearing at the High Court and questioned why he was being taken to EOCO. He said he asked for identification and an arrest warrant, which he claimed was not produced, before driving away because he feared for his safety. EOCO has maintained that parliamentary membership does not, by itself, bring an investigation to an end or place an individual beyond the reach of the law, while stressing that it would respect constitutional parliamentary privileges. Article 118(2) further provides that a certificate from the Speaker stating that an MP or the Clerk is attending parliamentary proceedings is conclusive evidence of attendance. Mr Anyenini said the current controversy highlights the need for greater clarity on when Article 117 protections apply. “But generally, my position has been that the returning from any proceedings of Parliament. My view is that they have abused it just too much,” he said. “Sometimes they are in their bedrooms, and then they will claim that they are attending to Parliament, and they are attending to the business of Parliament. You know, it’s a difficult thing, so we need to be clear about some of these things.”

items.title: Nations unies : « L’Afrique doit être à la table, pas au menu » (Antonio Guterres)
items.description: L’Afrique doit obtenir une place permanente au conseil de sécurité des Nations unies. C’est l’appel lancé par le secrétaire général de l’ONU, Antonio Guterres, lors de l’ouverture du débat général de la 81ᵉ session de l’Assemblée générale, le 22 septembre 2026 à New York. Selon le secrétaire général de l’ONU, António Guterres, l’absence de représentation permanente africaine ne correspond plus aux réalités géopolitiques actuelles. « L’Afrique doit être à la table, pas au menu », a-t-il déclaré, appelant les États membres à rendre le conseil de sécurité plus représentatif et plus légitime. L’Afrique ne dispose actuellement d’aucun siège permanent, alors même que le continent est directement concerné par plusieurs dossiers majeurs traités par le conseil, notamment les questions de paix et de sécurité. Pour rappel, le conseil compte actuellement 15 membres, dont cinq permanents disposant du droit de veto : les États-Unis, la Russie, la Chine, la France et le Royaume-Uni. Minute.bf

items.title: A l’ONU, le Burkina appelle à la fin des inégalités et à une réforme de l’architecture financière internationale
items.description: (New-York, le 23 septembre 2026) Les travaux de la 81e Assemblée générale des Nations Unies se sont poursuivis ce 23 septembre avec plusieurs réunions de haut niveau, dont celle relative à la commémoration du 40e anniversaire de la Déclaration des Nations Unies de 1986 sur le droit au développement. Le ministre des Affaires étrangères qui a livré la déclaration du Burkina Faso à cette occasion, a salué la tenue de cet évènement tout en déplorant la persistance de profondes inégalités entre les nations et au sein des sociétés. Devant l'assistance, il a présenté la vision du Burkina Faso sur le développement, qui doit reposer sur la liberté de définir sa propre voie pour un développement endogène, souverain et durable, à travers une production et une transformation locales des ressources, ainsi qu'un renforcement des capacités nationales. Il a présenté les résultats encourageants obtenus par le Burkina Faso grâce à cette vision et malgré les défis sécuritaires. >, a t-il déclaré. Le Chef de la diplomatie burkinabè a par ailleurs indiqué que les pays de la Confédération des États du Sahel assument pleinement leur responsabilité de protéger leurs peuples et leurs territoires. >, a martelé le Camarade ministre Karamoko Jean Marie TRAORE. Pour lui, lorsque les mécanismes de justice internationale sont dévoyés et utilisés comme des instruments de pression politique, leur crédibilité s’en trouve profondément affectée, et c'est dans ce contexte que les États membres de la Confédération des États du Sahel ont engagé leur retrait du Statut de Rome de la Cour pénale internationale. Pour terminer, il a souligné l’exigence d’une réforme de l’architecture financière internationale, d'une fiscalité plus équitable et le renforcement des capacités productives nationales, pour la réalisation du droit au développement. Cette réalisation exige également que le terrorisme, les ingérences ainsi que les atteintes à la souveraineté et à l’intégrité territoriale soient reconnus comme des entraves au développement. >, a conclu le ministre des Affaires étrangères. DCRP/MAE L’article A l'ONU, le Burkina appelle à la fin des inégalités et à une réforme de l’architecture financière internationale est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .
